title: The bedtime Shema
hook: before sleep: the Shema, and forgiveness for anyone who hurt you that day

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dayan HaEmet, three words inside grief, and then silence. Your line was even here, a word. Today, the last blessing of the day, and the last day of this part of the path. Day one hundred twenty.

Late at night, lights off. A tired body, and a mind still replaying the day. What she said in the meeting. The text he never answered. The driver who cut in. The comeback gets rewritten, again. Midnight, then one. A grudge makes a strange pillow, and plenty of nights end on one. Jewish tradition has a practice for exactly this hour, and its first step is letting go. Today: Modeh Ani, and its bookend.
screen: `THE LIGHTS ARE OFF.` → `REPLAYING THE DAY.` → `ASLEEP, HOLDING A GRUDGE.`

segments.voice: Way back in camp one, you learned the Shema, the line at the heart of Jewish prayer. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." And the Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." So Jews say the Shema in the evening prayers. But the Talmud says to say it again, in bed, right before sleep. It points to a line from the Psalms: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." Over the centuries, the bedtime Shema grew into a short bedtime service. Many prayer books begin it with a declaration. Before the Shema, before anything, a person says that they forgive anyone who angered or hurt them that day, in body, money, honor or anything else, whether by accident or on purpose, and asks that no one be punished on their account. The Talmud tells of a rabbi, Mar Zutra, who did this every night: before going to bed, he said, I forgive everyone who troubled me. Then comes the Shema, and a blessing thanking God, who lets sleep fall on my eyes. Many say a line from a psalm: "Into Thy hand I commit my spirit." And in many homes, children and adults say a line about four angels: Michael on my right, Gabriel on my left, Uriel in front, Raphael behind, and above my head, God's presence. Angels came up before, in the Friday-night song of welcome; at bedtime, four of them are named. So look at the shape of the day you've learned in this part of the path. It opens with thank you, Modeh Ani, before your feet touch the floor. It closes with I forgive you, before your eyes close. Blessings all the way through.
screen: `THE SHEMA, AGAIN, IN BED.` · `I FORGIVE ANYONE WHO HURT ME.` · `MAR ZUTRA, EVERY NIGHT.` · `FOUR ANGELS AROUND THE BED.` · then, large: `INTO THY HAND I COMMIT MY SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one thing before you sleep. Let's practice it now, so it's ready tonight. Settle, and breathe. Let one small hurt from today, or this week, come to mind. Not the biggest one. Something you can manage. Picture the person. You don't have to say they were right. You don't have to call them. Just set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor before bed. Say to yourself: I forgive this, for tonight. If you pray, you can hand it to God. The bell holds the time.
Modeh Ani, the morning thanks said before your feet touch the floor, the bookend to the bedtime Shema's forgiveness before sleep.
Your line: forgive before sleeping. Tonight, in bed, let one thing go before you close your eyes. Tomorrow a new part begins: the holidays, starting with the calendar. Day one hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Before sleep, many Jews say the bedtime Shema: a declaration forgiving anyone who wronged them, the Shema, the Hamapil blessing, and verses such as Psalm 31:6 and the line about the four angels.

trapdoor: what you thought: a child's bedtime prayer.
what it means: forgiveness first, then the Shema, then sleep in God's hand, closing a day that began with thank you.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 4b–5a (Shema on the bed, Psalm 4:5); Megillah 28a (Mar Zutra); the forgiveness text in its current form appears in later prayer books.

Last day of 'blessings through the day' (days 109–120); the teach bookends Modeh Ani and the bedtime Shema. The voice refers to learning the Shema 'back in camp one'; confirm the Shema was taught in days 1–21 (day 21 lists 'the Shema').

Editor review (days 113–131): hook no longer tells the listener what they do in bed ('you write your comeback', 'plenty of us fall asleep holding a grudge'), and 'its first step isn't a prayer' was cut, since the forgiveness declaration is itself a prayer text; 'something remarkable' stock phrase cut; 'the two angels who walked you home on Friday night… come back at bedtime' conflated the unnamed Shabbat angels (Shabbat 119b, Shalom Aleichem) with the four named angels, so it now just notes angels appeared before and four are named here.
